1.pericope_label: Likewise, ye wives, be in subjection to your own husbands; that, if any obey not the word, they also may without the word be won by the conversation of the wives; While they behold your chaste conversation coupled with fear. Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.

schools.summary: Note that the Greek is participial and hangs the instruction on the earlier commands to citizens and slaves, and raise the question whether it binds Christian wives for all time as completely, since the special reason here was to allay suspicions raised by a religion proclaiming individual freedom, and the same writer's command of absolute submission in slaves has since seen slavery abolished; observe that the possessive is strengthened by the article, so that submission is to a woman's own husband and no other's; deny that the passage is a corrective of vanity at all, reading it as an answer to how husbands are to be won; and refuse the received rendering of the contrast, which makes the hidden man an ornament worn instead of gold.

Find the point of the paragraph in the harder case, since wives married to unbelievers might seem to have a pretence for shaking off the yoke, and argue from the greater to the less — if such must obey ungodly husbands, much more promptly should those obey who have believing ones; then ask whether the prohibition of ornament is absolute and answer that it is not, since pressing the words would forbid precious things altogether when what is condemned is excess, a decent garb suitable to a person's years and rank being commendable.

Read the prohibition strictly, since three things are here expressly forbidden — curling the hair, wearing gold by way of ornament, and putting on costly or gay apparel — and these ought never to be allowed by Christians, much less defended; describe the practice being condemned from its history, plaiting and folding the hair about the head being the most ancient and simplest way of dressing it, still current in the east and known from gems and statues; and press the substitution home, that meekness and quietness are put in the room of the ornaments forbidden, since superfluity of dress feeds pride and anger more than is generally supposed.

Set the case in its social difficulty, that Christian matrons might imagine their conversion and their interest in Christian privileges exempted them from subjection to pagan or Jewish husbands, and answer that obliging conduct is the likeliest way to win a husband who has rejected the word and attends to no other evidence of its truth.

debates.question: Does the passage forbid ornament absolutely?

sides.position: Three things are expressly forbidden and ought never to be allowed by Christians, much less defended
Pressing the words would forbid precious things altogether; what is condemned is excess
Clothing is convenient and necessary, and a decent garb suitable to one's years and rank is commendable; the fault lies in luxury and immoderation
God does not condemn real ornament at all, the universe being full of it; the only question is what the true ornament is
The passage is not directly a corrective of vanity but an answer to how husbands are to be won

debates.question: How far does the command of wifely submission bind?

sides.position: It may be questioned whether it binds for all time as completely, since the special reason was to allay suspicion of a religion proclaiming freedom, and the parallel command to slaves has since seen slavery abolished
It binds the more where the husband is unbelieving, and much more promptly where he believes
Conversion and Christian privilege do not exempt a woman from subjection to a pagan husband

outliers.note: Alone defends ornament in principle, arguing that God does not condemn it since the universe is full of it in the colours of clouds and rainbow, the hues of flowers and the plumage of birds.

Alone raises the question whether the command of wifely submission binds for all time as completely as it is stated here, observing that the parallel injunction to slaves has since seen slavery abolished altogether.

themes: the hidden man of the heart

5.pericope_label: For after this manner in the old time the holy women also, who trusted in God, adorned themselves, being in subjection unto their own husbands: Even as Sara obeyed Abraham, calling him lord: whose daughters ye are, as long as ye do well, and are not afraid with any amazement. Likewise, ye husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered.

schools.summary: Take the appeal to antiquity as proof that God sets a value on such adorning, having accepted it in the holy women of old; press the word trusted, which stands where hoped belongs, since their position was one of expectancy looking to a promise, and read holy as meaning sainted, consecrated by having their memory recorded in Scripture; correct the clause about Sarah's daughters, which says not whose daughters ye are but whose children ye became, pointing to a definite moment in the past; and be careful that the wife's weakness is physical and not intellectual or moral.

Turn the verse about ancient simplicity into a complaint about the present, since natural ornaments alone were once used until trade brought in luxuries and luxury brought pride; hold that no female head looks so well as when adorned with its own hair, the ornament appointed by God; read the clause about Sarah's daughters as conditional, the relationship lasting no longer than belief and belief no longer than obedience; and take the closing warning about hindered prayer as reaching both parties, since all sin hinders prayer and anger particularly.

Observe how a single recorded word is made to stand for a habit, since God does not regard titles and even a petulant wife might use the word once, so that Sarah must have spoken thus usually, knowing herself commanded to be subject; then require prudence of husbands and state the condition plainly, that dominion is given only on terms of exercising authority prudently, so that many foolish and unpleasant things must be borne while indulgence is kept from fostering folly — and note that the two reasons given for honour, weakness and joint inheritance, seem contrary but agree well where love exists, since nothing destroys the friendship of life more than contempt.

debates.question: What does calling Abraham lord prove about Sarah?

sides.position: That she usually spoke thus, since God does not regard titles and even a petulant wife might use the word once
That her subjection was habitual, since she was not addressing Abraham but speaking to herself, and people show their habits of mind most freely then
That she acknowledged his superiority and her own subjection in the order of God, as the rabbinic parallel also reads it

debates.question: Is whose daughters ye are the right rendering?

sides.position: No: it is whose children ye became, pointing to a definite moment in the past, which suggests the readers were Gentiles
It is a standing relationship, conditional on continuance, since it cannot be maintained longer than belief lasts
It is spiritual as well as natural sonship, entitling them to the same inheritance

outliers.note: Alone turns the verse about ancient simplicity into a complaint about contemporary fashion, holding that to exchange the hair God gave for hair of another colour is an insult to the Creator.
Alone reads the command against fear as addressed to a specific temper, that women liable to be frightened often make much of a little thing and so raise commotions at home.

themes: heirs together of the grace of life

8.pericope_label: Finally, be ye all of one mind, having compassion one of another, love as brethren, be pitiful, be courteous: Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing. For he that will love life, and see good days, let him refrain his tongue from evil, and his lips that they speak no guile: Let him eschew evil, and do good; let him seek peace, and ensue it. For the eyes of the Lord are over the righteous, and his ears are open unto their prayers: but the face of the Lord is against them that do evil.

schools.summary: Note that the opening word concludes not the epistle but only the addresses to the various classes; observe how unusual the five virtues named are, three of them occurring nowhere else in the New Testament and one a late and rare compound; hold that the general precepts still serve the purpose the special ones did, since the impression made on unbelieving watchers was the object throughout; and find in the quotation a deliberate change of sense rather than a lapse of memory, the psalmist having asked merely who desires to live while the apostle asks who cares for a life worth having.

Notice an absence in the preceding rules, that the duty of masters towards their servants is omitted, and refuse the inference that there were no Christian masters among the readers, since Paul specifies that duty to churches in the same region; then admit that common feeling favours the opposite of what is here taught, men supposing they expose themselves to insolence if they do not boldly defend themselves, while the Spirit promises a happy life only to the meek and to those who endure evils.

Render the five virtues term by term as sympathetic, lovers of the brethren, tender-hearted so that the bowels yearn over the afflicted, and friendly-minded — while reporting that the last is probably not the true reading, a long list of manuscripts and versions giving humble-minded instead, which an editor has admitted into the text; define courtesy as such behaviour toward equals and inferiors as shows respect mixed with love; and reduce the quoted psalm to practical rules: refrain from slander, avoid flattery that covers wicked intention, keep going away from evil, do good, and seek peace where it has been lost.

Take the passage as teaching how Christians and friends should treat one another, and note the circumstance that gives the list its shape, that many of the readers were then in a suffering condition, which is why compassion and pity stand in it at all; and set the aim as being like-minded in the great points of faith, in real affection and in Christian practice.

debates.question: Is the fifth virtue courteous or humble-minded?

sides.position: Courteous is the received text, but humble-minded is probably the true reading, given by many manuscripts and versions and admitted into the text by Griesbach
Humble minded, a late compound found in Plutarch and Proverbs and nowhere else in the New Testament
Courtesy, meaning such behaviour toward equals and inferiors as shows respect mixed with love

debates.question: Why is the duty of masters omitted from the preceding rules?

sides.position: Not because there were no Christian masters among the readers, since Paul specifies that duty to churches in the same region; the omission is singular but not evidence
The general precepts now given cover all the relations previously specified

outliers.note: Alone notices that the duty of masters towards servants is missing from the preceding rules, and disposes of the inference that no Christian masters were among the readers.
Alone reduces the quoted psalm to five numbered rules of conduct, ending with seeking peace where it has been lost and restoring it where it has been broken.

themes: be ye all of one mind

13.pericope_label: And who is he that will harm you, if ye be followers of that which is good? But and if ye suffer for righteousness’ sake, happy are ye: and be not afraid of their terror, neither be troubled; But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear: Having a good conscience; that, whereas they speak evil of you, as of evildoers, they may be ashamed that falsely accuse your good conversation in Christ. For it is better, if the will of God be so, that ye suffer for well doing, than for evil doing.

schools.summary: Observe that the sentence is framed as a remote possibility, using a mood already dying out of the language, so that the sense is if matters should after all come to actual suffering — and that suffering here means much more than harm, namely the horrors of capital punishment, mentioned as a case well supposable rather than as impending; then settle the great textual question, that the true reading is sanctify the Lord the Christ and not the Lord God, and draw the inference that a Jew could not have applied the prophet's words about the Lord of hosts to a man he had known familiarly unless the doctrine states a fact; and recover the old force of the word for answer, a defence rather than an excuse.

State the prior point that kindness does more towards a quiet life than violence and quickness to revenge, so that the blessing belongs to those who suffer after neglecting nothing for peace; and add the qualification that keeps the command to answer from becoming indiscriminate, since the apostle does not bid us proclaim everywhere, always and to all alike, the Lord giving his people a spirit of discretion by which they may know when and how far and to whom it is expedient to speak, and bidding them only be ready.

Join the two conditions of the answer, that we should be able to defend our religion with meekness and in the fear of God, and observe that where this great fear is there is no room for other fears, since it does not disturb; then state the comparison of the last verse plainly, that it is better to suffer for well-doing than for evil-doing whatever our natural impatience may suggest, since the man on whom sin and suffering meet together is in a sad condition, sin making the suffering extreme and comfortless and destructive.

Find the happiness in the cause rather than the experience, since a man who was not holy would not be persecuted at all, so that he is happy in the very ground of his sufferings; and ask what sanctifying God can possibly mean, since to sanctify is to make holy and God cannot be made so — answering that the sense is to entertain just notions of him and to separate him in the heart from everything earthly, human, fickle, rigidly severe or capriciously merciful.

debates.question: Is the true reading sanctify the Lord God or the Lord the Christ?

sides.position: The Lord the Christ, without a shadow of doubt — and a Jew could not have applied the prophet's words about the Lord of hosts to a man he had known familiarly unless the doctrine states a fact
Christ as Lord, an adaptation of Isaiah to Christ, not the God of the received text
The Lord God, glossed from the prophet as regarding him as protector and fearing him rather than what man can do
The Lord God, though sanctifying him can only mean entertaining just notions of him and separating him in the heart from everything earthly and capricious

outliers.note: Alone builds a christological argument out of the textual variant, asking how a Jew could have applied to a man he had known familiarly the prophet’s words about the Lord of hosts.
Alone limits the command to give an answer, holding that the Lord gives his people a spirit of discretion by which they may know when and how far and to whom it is expedient to speak.

18.pericope_label: For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit: By which also he went and preached unto the spirits in prison; Which sometime were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing, wherein few, that is, eight souls were saved by water.

schools.summary: Read the appeal to Christ's suffering as argument from precedent, since it is some ease to the mind in distress to look on examples of the like or greater distress, and note that the title used here is King Messiah rather than Jesus; then handle the hardest verse in the epistle honestly, setting out the two main lines of interpretation and deciding the preceding phrase in favour of taking in spirit to mean out of the body; report that Luther admitted he did not know what the passage means, and list the escapes attempted, including a conjectural emendation reading Noah also or Enoch also which has no manuscript behind it; and observe that the word disobedient describes not all sinners but those who heard and were convinced and still refused.

Draw a second comfort from the design rather than the fact of that death, that Christ suffered to bring us to God, so that we are consecrated to him and cannot consistently suffer for our own evil deeds; then reject the common reading of the difficult verse, since it has been found to teach a descent into hell while the words say no such thing, no mention being made of Christ's soul but only that he went by the Spirit; and admit the real difficulty, that the verse names not the faithful but the unbelieving, answering it from the next chapter where the gospel is said to have been preached to the dead that they might live according to God in the spirit.

Hold that the preaching was by the ministry of Noah over a hundred and twenty years, and that the antediluvians are called imprisoned because, tried and convicted, they were detained under the arrest of divine justice while it waited either for their repentance or for the expiry of their respite; and add that they are reserved still to the judgment of the great day.

Set out the argument for patience in stages: that Christ was not exempted from suffering though he had no guilt of his own and could have declined it; that the meritorious cause was the sins of men, the punishment being true and proper and offered to expiate sin; and that in his case the just suffered for the unjust, he substituting himself in our room and bearing our iniquities.

debates.question: Who were the spirits in prison, and when were they preached to?

sides.position: The antediluvians, preached to by the ministry of Noah over a hundred and twenty years, imprisoned in the sense of being held under the arrest of divine justice awaiting repentance or the expiry of their respite
Spirits preached to after Christ's death, in spirit meaning out of the body, as a disembodied spirit
Not a descent into hell, since no mention is made of Christ's soul but only that he went by the Spirit
The event took place between the death and the resurrection
The text is corrupt and originally read Noah also or Enoch also — a conjecture with no manuscript behind it, rejected as inconsistent with the context

outliers.note: Alone reports the history of scholarly despair over the passage, including Luther’s admission that he did not know what it means and a conjectural emendation, unsupported by any manuscript, that would insert the name of Noah or Enoch.
Alone identifies the suffering in view as the horrors of capital punishment, and observes that it is raised as a case well supposable rather than as something already occurring.

21.pericope_label: The like figure whereunto even baptism doth also now save us (not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God,) by the resurrection of Jesus Christ: Who is gone into heaven, and is on the right hand of God; angels and authorities and powers being made subject unto him.

schools.summary: Settle the antecedent before anything else, since the relative is neuter and cannot agree with the feminine word for ark but does agree with the neuter word for water; find two false readings in the received sentence, the easier whereunto standing where the harder which belongs and us where the text has you, and prefer to make the water rather than the baptism the subject, since calling the Flood point-blank a baptism is difficult; insist that the salvation by baptism here is symbolic, a metaphor or picture rather than an actual thing, as the next clause hastens to explain; and read the closing verse as partly a doxology which carries the history forward in order and teaches the believer's entire conformity to his Lord.

Judge that the case of the relative has been corrupted and ought to be read in the dative, though the meaning is not thereby made ambiguous, Noah saved by water having had a sort of baptism; make the burial the point of the figure, since in baptism we are buried with Christ so that, dead to the world and the flesh, we may live to God; and take the two clauses of the last verse as answering two temptations, the ascension commended lest our eyes seek Christ in the world and the session lest we doubt his power to save, since sitting at the right hand means exercising supreme power everywhere as God's representative.

Distinguish sign from thing signified, since it is not the bare outward sign that saves but the inward grace, a consciousness that both our persons and our actions are accepted; and report the curious addition found after the clause about the right hand of God in the Latin and some other versions and in several Latin fathers — swallowing up death, that we might be made heirs of eternal life — while noting that it stands in no Greek copy at all.

Declare what saving baptism means and what it does not, since it is not the outward ceremony of washing with water, which in itself does no more than put away the filth of the flesh, but the baptism in which there is a faithful answer of a resolved good conscience, engaging to believe in and be devoted to God while renouncing the flesh, the world and the devil — washing being the visible sign and this the thing signified.

debates.question: What is the antecedent of the relative in the baptism verse?

sides.position: Water, not the ark, since the relative is neuter and the word for ark is feminine
Water, and the relative should be read in the dative, the case having been corrupted
Water, the harder reading which standing where the easier whereunto has been substituted, since calling the Flood point-blank a baptism is difficult

debates.question: In what sense does baptism save?

sides.position: Symbolically only, as a metaphor or picture and not actually
Not by the outward ceremony, which of itself only puts away the filth of the flesh, but by the faithful answer of a resolved good conscience
Not by the bare outward sign but by the inward grace, a consciousness that our persons and actions are accepted

outliers.note: Alone itemises the correspondences that make the ark a figure of baptism — that it was God’s ordinance and not man’s invention, that it was the scorn of men while it was preparing, and that Noah shut into it represented a burial.
Alone reports in full the addition found after the clause about the right hand of God in the Latin and other versions and in several Latin fathers, while noting that it stands in no Greek copy.

themes: the answer of a good conscience
on the right hand of God
